messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am conducting measurement invariance across 4 timepoints. I have a latent factor of "depression" composed of 5 items (binary). I am able to converge and obtain good fit for configural and metric invariance. However, I cannot converge my scalar model. I've tried reducing missing data by using imputation and also increased the number of iterations but it still will not converge.

I'm wondering whether this is an issue with my code, or simply the data does not achieve scalar invariance. See my code below - really appreciate any help!:

#define scalar model
dep_scalar_model <- '
# Constraints factorial loadings to be equal across time points
dep1 =~ V1Loading*mood1 + V2Loading*anhe1 + V3Loading*guil1 + V4Loading*hope1 + V5Loading*apat1

dep2 =~ V1Loading*mood2 + V2Loading*anhe2 + V3Loading*guil2 + V4Loading*hope2 + V5Loading*apat2

dep3 =~ V1Loading*mood3 + V2Loading*anhe3 + V3Loading*guil3 + V4Loading*hope3 + V5Loading*apat3

dep4 =~ V1Loading*mood4 + V2Loading*anhe4 + V3Loading*guil4 + V4Loading*hope4 + V5Loading*apat4

# Allow covariance between latent factors throughtout time
dep1 ~~ dep2 + dep3 + dep4
dep2 ~~ dep3 + dep4
dep3 ~~ dep4

# Allow covariance between errors of the same variables throughout time
mood1 ~~ mood2 + mood3 + mood4
anhe1 ~~ anhe2 + anhe3 + anhe4
guil1 ~~ guil2 + guil3 + guil4
hope1 ~~ hope2 + hope3 + hope4
apat1 ~~ apat2 + apat3 + apat4

# Constrain thresholds to be equal across time points
mood1 | t1
mood2 | t1
mood3 | t1
mood4 | t1

anhe1 | t2
anhe2 | t2
anhe3 | t2
anhe4 | t2

guil1 | t3
guil2 | t3
guil3 | t3
guil4 | t3

hope1 | t4
hope2 | t4
hope3 | t4
hope4 | t4

apat1 | t5
apat2 | t5
apat3 | t5
apat4 | t5
'

# Fit
fit_scalar <- cfa(dep_scalar_model, data = dass,
                      ordered = c("mood1", "anhe1", "guil1", "hope1", "apat1",
                                     "mood2", "anhe2", "guil2", "hope2", "apat2",
                                     "mood3", "anhe3", "guil3", "hope3", "apat3",
                                     "mood4", "anhe4", "guil4", "hope4", "apat4"),
                      parameterization = "theta", estimator = "wlsmv",
                      missing = "pairwise",
                      control = list(iter.max = 10000,  # Increase max iterations
                               rel.tol = 1e-5))

> What did I do wrong? Error says:  error: lavaan->lav_lavaan_step01_ovnames_checklv(): some latent variable names collide with observed variable names: f1 f2

Hmm, it seems I didn't plan for higher-order factors.  Early in the function, the syntax objects are parsed into parameter tables, to match observed-variable names and parcel names that measure the same factor.  I updated the syntax to remove any latent-variable names (i.e., variables ever appearing on the left-hand side of the =~ operator) from either list.  This should suffice to:
distinguish parcels from latent variables on the right-hand side of the =~ operator
only create parcels from observed variables.
You can install the updated semTools from GitHub:

remotes::install_github("simsem/semTools/semTools")

After which, this reprex works fine:

library(semTools) # already loads lavaan

item.syntax <- c(paste0("f1 =~ f1item", 1:9),
                 paste0("f2 =~ f2item", 1:9),

                 paste0("f3 =~ f1 + f2"))

## 3-indicator parcels
mod.parcels <- '
  f1 =~ par1 + par2 + par3
  f2 =~ par4 + par5 + par6

  f3 =~ L1*f1 + L1*f2 # constrain loadings to equality, so model is identified

'
## names of parcels
(parcel.names <- paste0("par", 1:6))

parcelAllocation(mod.parcels, data = simParcel, nAlloc = 5,

                 parcel.names = parcel.names, item.syntax = item.syntax,

                 std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE)

>  anx1 =~ W1Loading*worr1 + W2Loading*ganx1 + W3Loading*irri1 + W4Loading*rest1

To be safe, you should specify a vector for each parameter (1 label per group), making them the same label for each group to impose equality constraints across groups.  But the default should be to repeat a single label for each group, when only 1 is provided.

> # Allow covariance between errors of the same variables throughout time
>   worr1 ~~ worr2 + worr3
>   ganx1 ~~ ganx2 + ganx3
>   irri1 ~~ irri2 + irri3
>   rest1 ~~ rest2 + rest3

What about between times 2 and 3?

  worr2 ~~ worr3
  ganx2 ~~ ganx3
  irri2 ~~ irri3
  rest2 ~~ rest3

>   # Constraints intercepts to be equal across time points

Those are thresholds (the | operator), not intercepts (~1).

> fit_scalar_anx <- cfa(anx_scalar_model, data = elsa_merge_anx,
>                   group = "cohort",
>                   group.equal = c("loadings", "thresholds"),

To be clear, group.equal= should also include intercepts, but by default they will all be fixed to 0 anyway (thus equal across groups and time).

>                   ordered = c("worr1", "ganx1", "irri1", "rest1",
>                               "worr2", "ganx2", "irri2", "rest2",
>                               "worr3", "ganx3", "irri3", "rest3"),

If this is all the manifest indicators in your model, a shortcut is merely ordered=TRUE

https://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/cat.html

messages.body_plain:
For the first question: as soon as missing = "(fi)ml" is used, lavaan
now attempts to compute a 'robust' CFI/RMSEA value. The reason for this
is well explained in this paper:

Zhang, X., & Savalei, V. (2023). New computations for RMSEA and CFI
following FIML and TS estimation with missing data. Psychological
Methods, 28(2), 263-283. https://doi.org/10.1037/met0000445

In short: the more missing values you have, the better the (non-robust)
fit measures get.... (a dirty secret some people have misused).

For the second question: when missing = "(fi)ml", the observed 'mean
vector' is estimated using the EM algorithm. When the mean structure is
saturated, it will be very close, but often not identical to the
model-implied 'mean vector'.

Yves.

messages.body_plain:
A new R package is available on CRAN <https://cran.r-project.org/package=lavaan.mi>, which contains some familiar but greatly improved functionality that is now deprecated from semTools 0.5-7 <https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=semTools>.  Among the improvements is a stronger consistency in the user interface between lavaan and lavaan.mi, including new *.mi() functions listed in the README <https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/lavaan.mi/readme/README.html> description.  The NEWS <https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/lavaan.mi/news/news.html> file includes a list of changes that make this package differ from the semTools functionality.  I also attached my presentation slides from the recent PsychoCo workshop <https://www.psychoco.org/2025/index.html>, which provide a good overview of the package's functionality.

The semTools package still supports lavaan.mi-class objects, but until the deprecated semTools functions are completely removed from a future version of semTools, you should always load the packages in the following order:

library(semTools)
library(lavaan.mi)

Note that either line automatically first loads lavaan because it is a dependency for both packages.  So a separate library(lavaan) call is not necessary.

Best,

messages.subject: semTools 0.5-7 on CRAN
messages.subject_clean: semTools 0.5-7 on CRAN
messages.body_plain:
For the first time since May 2022, a new version of semTools (0.5-7) is on CRAN <https://cran.r-project.org/package=semTools>.  It may be a day or two before a binary is built for your OS, but you can read about nearly 3-years worth of new features and bug fixes here <https://github.com/simsem/semTools/blob/master/semTools/NEWS.md>.  There are 2 suites of features <https://github.com/simsem/semTools/wiki/Functions> that have been deprecated:
EFA functionality will soon be removed because it is now available in lavaan <https://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/efa.html>
The runMI() function will soon be removed, and all supporting functionality for lavaan.mi-class objects has been moved to its own R package: lavaan.mi, which I also posted about here <https://groups.google.com/g/lavaan/c/n2_5BZkDC8w/m/A339xki9AQAJ>.
Although there do not appear to be any explicit semTools reverse-dependencies specifically due to runMI(), I know there are people who use semTools to teach SEM, and have depended on runMI() for years.  So I expect the removal of runMI() from semTools to create a major (albeit temporary) disruption for a few people.
GOOD NEWS: The new lavaan.mi package is designed to have a more familiar interface for lavaan users, by minimizing differences between fitting a lavaan() model to 1 data set and fitting lavaan.mi() to a list of imputed data sets.  The set of generic methods is available in the README <https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/lavaan.mi/readme/README.html> description, as well as a table listing all lavaan functions and their analogues; for example, parameterEstimates() and standardizedSolution() are available as parameterEstimates.mi() and standardizedSolution.mi().  Note that these expand what was available from semTools; lavResiduals.mi() is another new function.
CHALLENGING NEWS:
The runMI() function has been removed altogether, so the baseline function is simply lavaan.mi(), similar to lavaan() itself.
It is no longer possible to request multiple imputation via Amelia or mice when calling lavaan.mi(); you are expected to impute the data first (using whatever R or external software you prefer) and pass a list of imputed data sets to lavaan.mi().
When calling anova() or any lavTest*.mi() functions, the test= argument in semTools has been changed to pool.method= (e.g., to request D2, D3, or newly available D4).  The latter update is necessary to accommodate lavaan's lavTestLRT(test=) argument, which allows users to select which specific scaled(-shifted) test statistic to calculate, and thus which pooled robust statistic is returned by lavTestLRT.mi().
If any of these changes require immediately updating your teaching materials, please consult the Differences from semTools list in the NEWS <https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/lavaan.mi/news/news.html> file, as well as the README <https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/lavaan.mi/readme/README.html> description.  I tried to be exhaustive and informative enough for teachers to benefit, but if you encounter a struggle not sufficiently addressed in the NEWS <https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/lavaan.mi/news/news.html> or README <https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/lavaan.mi/readme/README.html> descriptions, please Reply-All to this post with questions or difficulties related to updating your materials from semTools to lavaan.mi.  I am not able to post on this forum as often as I used to, but I will keep an eye out for replies to this specific post.

Finally, to avoid conflicts in generic methods between packages, runMI() now returns an OLDlavaan.mi-class object, and semTools methods are defined for that class.  However, if you plan to use other semTools features during the same analysis (e.g., a single R script) as you use lavaan.mi, then there will be a conflict as long as the runMI() functionality remains deprecated (i.e., both packages contain lavaan.mi() and lavTest*.mi() functions, etc.).  Until the old functions are completely removed from a future version of semTools, you should always load the packages in the following order:

library(semTools)
library(lavaan.mi)

Note that either line automatically first loads lavaan because it is a dependency for both packages.  But loading semTools first means that its older *.mi() functions will be "masked" when lavaan.mi is subsequently loaded.  That's what you want for a less complicated experience.  If semTools is loaded when lavaan.mi is already in the search() path (also appearing in sessionInfo() output), then there is a "splash" message in your Console warning that the lavaan.mi functions are masked, and provides some syntax to detach and reattach lavaan.mi to correct this.

Overall, I am hopeful that these changes will be positive in the long term, even if a short-term adjustment period has a bit of difficulty.

Good luck with using the new packages in your research!

Terrence D. Jorgensen  (he, him, his)
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.subject_clean: Schmid-Leiman transformation of exploratory bifactor model
messages.body_plain:
I'm interested in estimating an exploratory bifactor model. My understanding from Giordano and Waller (2020; citation below) is that it is preferable to perform a Schmid-Leiman or Direct Schmid-Leiman transformation. How can I do that using an exploratory bifactor model that was estimated using lavaan?

Giordano, C., & Waller, N. G. (2020). Recovering bifactor models: A comparison of seven methods. Psychological Methods, 25(2), 143–156. https://doi.org/10.1037/met0000227

Here’s a minimal reproducible example of an exploratory bifactor model:

library("lavaan")
library("simstandard")

model_fixed <- '
   Verbal =~ .5*V1 + .6*V2 + .7*V3
   Spatial =~ .7*S1 + .7*S2 + .6*S3
   Quant =~ .5*Q1 + .7*Q2 + .5*Q3
   Verbal ~~ .7*Spatial + .6*Quant
   Spatial ~~ .5*Quant
'

bifactor_data <- simstandard::sim_standardized(
     model_fixed,
     n = 10000,
     observed = TRUE,
     latent = FALSE,
     errors = FALSE)

exploratoryBifactor_syntax <- '
     efa("efa1")*f1 +
     efa("efa1")*f2 +
     efa("efa1")*f3 =~
        V1 + V2 + V3 +
        S1 + S2 + S3 +
        Q1 + Q2 + Q3

     g =~
        NA*V1 + V2 + V3 +
        S1 + S2 + S3 +
        Q1 + Q2 + Q3
'

exploratoryBifactor_model <- sem(
       exploratoryBifactor_syntax,
       data = bifactor_data,
       rotation = "geomin",
       missing = "ML",
       estimator = "MLR"
)

Thanks in advance!

> Error in lavaan.mi::lavaan.mi(model = f1, data = imp2final, rotation = "oblimin",  :
>   efa()* blocks detected in model= syntax. (Un)rotated factors cannot be matched across imputations, threatening validity of pooled results.

So the answer to your second question:

> I am wondering if I could subset from the imputed datasets the variables I intend to use for EFA, use the poolSat() function

is "yes".  There are references on the help page you can read for details, and there is example syntax showing you how it works.
It is meant to provide a set of arguments that are all passed to lavaan(data=), so replace fa() with lavaan's efa() in your syntax.
https://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/efa.html

If you only pass the pooled covariance matrix, then your SEs and test statistics cannot be trusted because they ignore the additional uncertainty due to missing data.  The poolSat() function also returns the NACOV= and WLS.V= arguments, which pool both the within- and between-imputation sampling (co)variances (read the help-page references for details).

I think you can still just use fa.parallel() for your parallel analysis, since you don't draw inferences from that (only establish a baseline for determining how many factors efa() should extract).

Bootstrapping a CI is about inference from sample to population, not about interpreting the point estimate. Hi Ayesha,

If you run:

summary(NCSC_CFA_himodel_gr_fit, fit.measures = TRUE, standardized=TRUE, rsquare=TRUE)

for the model in the reprex and look at the NC =~LG and SC =~sim estimates in the output, you will see that these estimates (and their associated standard errors) are unrealistically high compared to other estimates in the model. Although the model seems to have converged (NCSC_CFA_himodel_gr_fit@optim$converged), it looks like there were some problems with the estimation. Pasting only the relevant part of the output below:

Group 1 [A]:

Latent Variables:

                   Estimate  Std.Err  z-value  P(>|z|)   Std.lv  Std.all

  NC =~

    PS                1.772    0.993    1.786    0.074    0.871    0.871

    AWM               1.187    0.333    3.567    0.000    0.765    0.765

    LG               98.227   35.403    2.775    0.006    1.000    1.000

  SC =~

    sim              82.090   39.173    2.096    0.036    1.000    1.000

    ment              0.999    0.316    3.163    0.002    0.707    0.707

If you fit a multigroup model only for data from groups B and C, all robust fit measures (including the CFI and RMSEA) are computed as expected:

# run model WITHOUT group A included

NCSC_CFA_himodel_grBC_fit <- cfa(NCSC_CFA_himodel, data = himodel_df[himodel_df$group != "A",],

                                 group="group", std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE, estimator = "MLR", missing = "ml")

summary(NCSC_CFA_himodel_grBC_fit, fit.measures = TRUE, standardized=TRUE, rsquare=TRUE)

However, if you fit a single-group model only for Group A, model estimation fails and no fit measures are computed (also, estimates for NC =~LG and SC =~sim are unrealistically high):

# run single-group model ONLY with group A

NCSC_CFA_himodel_grA_fit <- cfa(NCSC_CFA_himodel, data = himodel_df[himodel_df$group == "A",],

summary(NCSC_CFA_himodel_grA_fit, fit.measures = TRUE, standardized=TRUE, rsquare=TRUE)

Warning message:

lavaan->lav_object_summary():

   fit measures not available if model did not converge

My guess is that this is due to a small sample size within Group A (110 people) relative to the model size (54 parameters). I would also check whether the same factor structure applies across groups.

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I tried using the NA's to specify that the loadings should be estimated freely. It does not appear to make a difference, even if I specify all the loadings to be estimated freely with NA.  I have ran the code pasted below several times which generates a random correlation matrix that I used to fit the models with. Sometimes it estimates the loadings freely and sometimes it gets constraint to 1 or -1. So my worry is that the structure of the matrix determines whether all the loadings can be estimated freely.

The data I used before I verifying this with the simulated data are based on median correlations from a posterior distribution, so perhaps it will be able to estimate the loadings better if they are fitted for every posterior iteration.

So I think the code itself isn't wrong, but it's mostly determined by the data used to fit the models. If anyone has further input on this I would love to hear it!

All the best,
Corné

``` r
#===============================================================================
# Create cor & cov matrices:
library(Matrix)

# Total number of traits
N_traits <- 6

# Define variances for each trait
variances <- runif(N_traits, min = 0.1, max = 1)

# Create variance-covariance matrix
cor_matrix <- matrix(0, nrow = N_traits, ncol = N_traits)

# Number of correlations
n_cors <- (N_traits * (N_traits - 1)) / 2

# Randomly generated correlation values
cor_values <- runif(n_cors, min = -0.9, max = 0.9)

# Populate the matrix with correlations
cor_matrix[upper.tri(cor_matrix)] <- cor_values
cor_matrix[lower.tri(cor_matrix)] <- t(cor_matrix)[lower.tri(cor_matrix)]
diag(cor_matrix) <- rep(1, N_traits)

# Ensure the correlation matrix is positive semi-definite
if (!all(eigen(cor_matrix)$values > 0)) {
  # Force the correlation matrix to be positive definite
  cor_matrix <- as.matrix(Matrix::nearPD(cor_matrix, corr = TRUE)$mat)
}

# Convert correlation matrix to a covariance matrix
std_devs <- sqrt(variances)
cov_matrix <- cor_matrix * (std_devs %o% std_devs)

# Ensure the covariance matrix is positive semi-definite
if (!all(eigen(cov_matrix)$values > 0)) {
  # Force the covariance matrix to be positive definite
  cov_matrix <- as.matrix(Matrix::nearPD(cov_matrix, corr = FALSE)$mat)
}

#===============================================================================
# SEM models

library(lavaan)
```

messages.subject: RI-CLPM - random intercept negative variance and the right model
messages.subject_clean: RI-CLPM - random intercept negative variance and the right model
messages.body_plain:
I am modelling data from a 3 time point longitudinal study using an RI-CLPM approach. There was a negative variance estimate for the between participant random intercept term for the outcome variable body weight (var_free model). The explanatory variable was a food addiction score (x) with the random intercept variance being more realistic.

This was a gross failure of the model in reflecting the nature of variability in the data as the between participant variance for weight was large as judged by alternative analyses. The within participant component of variance at time 1 was 812. That is all the between participant variability was being reflected in the within component. An alternative model was chosen in which the variance for the random intercept was fixed at 790, a sensible value based on other analyses carried out (var_fixed model).

Although the model fit measures were similar for both models the parameter estimates for autoregressive and cross-lagged terms were quite different. I decided that the var_fixed model would be a better model for representating the data. The attached html file contains all the analyses, details and explanations behind my analyses (including this post at the of the markdown document).

I have two questions.

Is my decision to choose the var_fixed model over the var_free model sound?

Was there some other way I could have fitted the model to overcome the negative variance estimation issue and not have to resort to fixing the between participant variance parameter?
Thanks, Kim

messages.body_plain:
Hi lavaan group,

I am trying to test a moderated mediation model that utilizes multilevel data (individuals in teams) and has a binary categorical moderator coded as 0 or 1. I am specifically interested in finding the indirect and direct effect sizes.

In other mediation models I've tested, I've used the average of the moderator +/- 1 SD to get the high and the low values, but with this model, the moderator is binary (0/1). To calculate the effect sizes, am I able to directly use a 0 or 1 in my calculations (see picture below) or do I need to use a different approach?

Here is an image of the model:

And the code I am currently using, where 0 and 1 have been plugged in directly for calculating effect sizes:

Thank you for your help!

Here is the code as text for reference:
path_model_1 <- '

Mediator_T2 ~ a1*IV + a2*Moderator + a3*IV:Moderator
DV ~ c1*IV + c2*Moderator + c3*IV:Moderator + b*Mediator

indirect.effect.mod_equals_0 :=(a1+a3*0)*(b)
indirect.effect.mod_equals_1 :=(a1+a3*1)*(b)
indirect.effect.difference := indirect.effect.mod_equals_0 - indirect.effect.mod_equals_1

direct.effect.mod_equals_0 :=c1+c3*0
direct.effect.mod_equals_1 :=c1+c3*1
direct.effect.difference := direct.effect.mod_equals_0 - direct.effect.mod_equals_1

total.effect.mod_equals_0 := direct.effect.mod_equals_0 + indirect.effect.mod_equals_0
total.effect.mod_equals_1 := direct.effect.mod_equals_1 + indirect.effect.mod_equals_1
total.effect.difference := total.effect.mod_equals_0 - total.effect.mod_equals_1

'

fit_path_model_1 <- sem(model = path_model_1, data = path_model_data_1,
                        cluster = "Team_assignment", bootstrap = 5000)
summary(fit_path_model_1, fit.measures = TRUE)

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

My advisor and I are conducting measurement invariance tests for a CFA model across male and female students. The RMSEA and chi-square model fit goodness-of-fit indices are not matching between the same model run in R lavaan and MPlus. However, the AIC/BIC, loglikelihood and chi-square test for baseline do match across outputs. Attached are screenshots to document these differences. Any help or clarification as to why these outputs would be different and what can be done to match the R lavaan output to MPlus would be much appreciated!

Here is the R lavaan code:
# set up the CFA model
model <- '
  F1 =~ VS99 + VS94 + VS104 + VS95 + VS108 + VS109
  VS99 ~ VS95
  VS99 ~ VS94
  VS95 ~ VS104
  VS94 ~ VS95
  VS108 ~ VS104
  VS104 ~ VS94
'
# test model separately for male and female students
fit <- cfa(model = model, data = data_female, estimator = "ML")
summary(fit, fit.measures = TRUE, standardized = TRUE)
fitMeasures(fit, c("chisq", "df", "cfi", "tli", "rmsea","rmsea.ci.lower", "rmsea.ci.upper", "srmr"))
fit <- cfa(model = model, data = data_male, estimator = "ML")
summary(fit, fit.measures = TRUE, standardized = TRUE)
fitMeasures(fit, c("chisq", "df", "cfi", "tli", "rmsea","rmsea.ci.lower", "rmsea.ci.upper", "srmr"))

# configural
fit_configural <- cfa(model, data = data, group = "gender")
summary(fit_configural, fit.measures = TRUE)
fitMeasures(fit_configural, c("chisq", "df", "cfi", "tli", "rmsea","rmsea.ci.lower", "rmsea.ci.upper", "srmr"))

# metric
fit_metric <- cfa(model, data = data, group = "gender", group.equal = c("loadings"))
summary(fit_metric, fit.measures = TRUE)
fitMeasures(fit_metric, c("chisq", "df", "cfi", "tli", "rmsea","rmsea.ci.lower", "rmsea.ci.upper", "srmr"))

# scalar
fit_scalar <- cfa(model, data = data, group = "gender", group.equal = c("loadings", "intercepts"))
summary(fit_scalar, fit.measures = TRUE)
fitMeasures(fit_scalar, c("chisq", "df", "cfi", "tli", "rmsea","rmsea.ci.lower", "rmsea.ci.upper", "srmr"))

# strict
fit_strict <- cfa(model, data = data, group = "gender", group.equal = c("loadings", "intercepts", "residuals"))
summary(fit_strict, fit.measures = TRUE)
fitMeasures(fit_strict, c("chisq", "df", "cfi", "tli", "rmsea","rmsea.ci.lower", "rmsea.ci.upper", "srmr"))

## Compare Models
anova(fit_configural, fit_metric)
anova(fit_metric, fit_scalar)
anova(fit_scalar, fit_strict)

## Factor Variances for Population Heterogeneity
fit_variance <- cfa(model, data = data, group = "gender", group.equal = c("loadings", "intercepts", "lv.variances"))
fit_latent_mean <- cfa(model, data = data, group = "gender", group.equal = c("loadings", "intercepts", "lv.variances", "means"))
fitMeasures(fit_variance, c("chisq", "df", "cfi", "tli", "rmsea","rmsea.ci.lower", "rmsea.ci.upper", "srmr"))
fitMeasures(fit_latent_mean, c("chisq", "df", "cfi", "tli", "rmsea","rmsea.ci.lower", "rmsea.ci.upper", "srmr"))

anova(fit_variance, fit_latent_mean)

I conducted a CFA with a second-order factor for Wellbeing to validate my measurement model for an SEM. My model is structured as follows:
model_secondorder <-
 ' Wellbeing =~ Engagement_LV + Perseverance_LV + Optimism_LV + Connectedness_LV + Happiness_LV

Engagement_LV =~ EPOCH5_E1 + EPOCH7_E2 + EPOCH11_E3 + EPOCH12_E4 Perseverance_LV =~ EPOCH2_P1 + EPOCH9_P2 + EPOCH16_P3

Connectedness_LV =~ EPOCH1_C1 + EPOCH10_C2 + EPOCH14_C3 + EPOCH15_C4 Happiness_LV =~ EPOCH4_H1 + EPOCH6_H2 + EPOCH8_H3 + EPOCH18_H4 '

fit_secondorder <- cfa(model_secondorder, data = data, estimator = "MLR", orthogonal = TRUE, missing = "fiml", std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE)

For the descriptive statistics, I used sum scores of the manifest variables for each subscale. I calculated Cronbach’s alpha and McDonald’s omega using ci.reliability. Additionally, I computed a global Wellbeing score as the average of the five subdimension sum scores.

compRelSEM(fit_secondorder, higher = "Wellbeing", tau.eq = FALSE)

Optimism_LV: 0.714

Wellbeing: 0.787

reliabilityL2(fit_secondorder, "Wellbeing")

I get:

omegaL2: 0.9017477
partialOmegaL1: 0.9037898

The reliability values differ depending on the function used. Also, the subscale reliabilities are different from when I compute them separately with ci.reliability. Which values should I report?

Can I compute omega for the global Wellbeing sum score (the average of the subdimensions)? If so, which function should I use?

Thanks in advance for your help! :)

On 3/26/25 6:43 PM, Ayesha Rashidi wrote:
> If we set std.lv <http://std.lv> =
> FALSE or bounds = 'standard' for the current higher order model, do the
> nested models need to be re-run using the same syntax?

Preferably, yes.

> Additionally, is
> there a more appropriate solution between the two i.e. std.lv <http://std.lv>=FALSE or
> bounds='standard'?

If it works with std.lv <http://std.lv> = FALSE, that is to be preferred. It simply
changes the way we set the metric of the latent variables, and that is a
harmless operation. You can always report the standardized solution
afterwards.

The argument bounds = "standard" potentially affects several (free)
parameters. It forces the parameters to stay between pre-specified
upper/lower bounds, in order to facilitate convergence. I would argue
that it still results in a useful solution, even if one or more
parameters are estimated at the boundary.

A paper about this 'bounded estimation' can be found here:

https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/10705511.2021.1982716

Yves.
